subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: A kind of bacteria grows so that at time t seconds there are t³⁄² bacteria. Find the rate of growth at time t = 4 seconds.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IB (2026-27 edition), book p.214, chapter 10 APPLICATIONS OF DERIVATIVES, the RATE MEASURE sub-section, Very Short Answer question 11(i). Chapter 10 is printed as five un-numbered sub-sections inside one chapter box and each sub-section restarts its own numbering, so the sub-section is named here; this bank ships the whole chapter as ONE unit. **Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work** — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. PRINTED STEM DEFECT, RECORDED AND NOT SILENTLY CORRECTED: the book's stem gives the count in SECONDS (at time t sec there are t to the power 3/2 bacteria) and then asks for the rate of growth at t = 4 HOURS, while its own working substitutes t = 4 into the derivative. The two readings cannot both hold — with t in seconds, 4 hours is t = 14400, and the book does not use that number anywhere. The stem authored here therefore reads 't = 4 seconds', the only reading consistent with the formula and with the book's own substitution. The exponent is also written here in real Unicode (t³⁄²) rather than the ASCII transcription t^(3/2), per this bank's notation rule; the quantity is unchanged. recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say what rate of growth means here and what you differentiate.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Differentiate the count
steps.margin_note: First mark. This is a rate of growth question. The rate of growth is the derivative of the number of bacteria with respect to time. The power rule works on 3/2 exactly as on a whole number: 3/2 − 1 = 1/2, and t to the power 1/2 is √t.
steps.memory_tip: A fractional power follows the same rule as any other: multiply by the power, then subtract one from it.
lines: This is a rate of growth question, so differentiate the count with respect to time.
Let N = t³⁄² be the number of bacteria at time t seconds.

recall.must_convey: That the rate of growth is dN/dt, and that differentiating t³⁄² gives (3/2)√t.
accept: rate of growth is the derivative of the number with respect to time
differentiate t to the power three by two and get three by two root t
bring the three by two down and reduce the power to one by two
rate of growth ante d N by d t, differentiate cheyyali
the derivative is three by two times root t

steps.why: Rate of growth means the derivative of the population with respect to time, so the whole method is one use of the power rule on a fractional index.
common_mistakes: Reducing the power but writing t³⁄² again in the derivative.
Reading t³⁄² as (3/2)t and differentiating to 3/2.
Substituting t = 4 into t³⁄² and reporting 8, which is the count and not the rate.

steps.label: Substitute t = 4
steps.margin_note: Second mark. √4 = 2 exactly, so (3/2)(2) = 3 and the answer is a whole number. The unit is bacteria per second, because the count is differentiated with respect to time in seconds.
steps.memory_tip: At t = 4 the count is 8 and the rate is 3 — two different numbers from one question. Read which one is asked before starting.

lines.text: ∴ rate of growth at t = 4 sec is 3 bacteria per second

recall.must_convey: That substituting t = 4 gives (3/2)(2) = 3 bacteria per second.
accept: root four is two so three by two into two is three
the rate is three bacteria per second
put t equals four in three by two root t and get three
four substitute cheste three bacteria per second vasthundi
the answer is three per second

steps.why: The 2 from √4 cancels the 2 in the denominator, so the rate comes out as the exact whole number 3 with no rounding.
common_mistakes: Writing (3/2) × 4 = 6 by substituting into t instead of into √t.
Giving 8, the value of t³⁄² at t = 4, which is the number of bacteria and not the rate.
Leaving the answer without the unit bacteria per second.

insider_note: Differentiate t^(3/2) by the ordinary power rule to get (3/2)√t. Then substitute t = 4, giving 3.
